chapter_title: Basic Transformation & Manipulation in Edit Mode
chapter_summary:
Building upon our understanding of selecting mesh components, it's time to learn how to transform them. The same fundamental transformation tools you used in Object Mode – Move, Rotate, and Scale – are equally powerful, if not more so, in Edit Mode. The key difference is that now, instead of affecting the entire object, these operations only apply to your currently **selected vertices, edges, or faces**.

To **Move (Translate)** selected components, press `G`. Just like in Object Mode, you can then move your mouse to freely translate the selection, or press `X`, `Y`, or `Z` to constrain the movement to a specific axis. For example, `G` then `Z` will move your selection only along the Z-axis.
To **Rotate** selected components, press `R`. Again, you can freely rotate or constrain to an axis by pressing `X`, `Y`, or `Z`.
To **Scale** selected components, press `S`. Similarly, you can scale uniformly or along a specific axis (`X`, `Y`, or `Z`).

These transformations are incredibly versatile. Imagine you're modeling a character's face: you might select a group of vertices around the eye and scale them inwards to make the eye socket deeper, or move them slightly to adjust the brow line. The ability to manipulate individual components gives you granular control over your model's shape.

An important concept when transforming is **Transformation Orientation**. By default, Blender uses "Global" orientation, meaning transformations align with the world's X, Y, and Z axes. However, sometimes you need to move or rotate components relative to their own orientation. For instance, if you have a face on an angled surface, and you want to move it directly outwards from that surface, "Local" orientation (selected from the dropdown next to the transformation gizmos) will align the transformation axes with the selected component's normal. This is crucial for precise adjustments on non-axis-aligned geometry, common in complex game assets.

Another critical setting is the **Pivot Point**. This determines the center around which rotations and scales occur. You can select different pivot points from the dropdown menu in the header of the 3D Viewport (it looks like two overlapping circles with a dot in the middle).
*   **Median Point:** This is the average center of all selected components. It's often the default and most intuitive choice.
*   **Active Element:** If you have multiple components selected, the *last* component you selected (the "active" one, usually highlighted brighter) becomes the pivot. This is useful for aligning multiple elements to one.
*   **Individual Origins:** Each selected component rotates or scales around its *own* center. This is fantastic for creating arrays of objects or making individual adjustments without affecting the group's overall position.
*   **3D Cursor:** The transformation occurs around the 3D Cursor's position. You can place the 3D Cursor anywhere by `Shift + Right-Click`. This offers ultimate control over the pivot point.
*   **Bounding Box Center:** The center of the smallest box that can enclose all selected components. Similar to Median Point but calculated slightly differently.

A powerful tool for organic modeling is **Proportional Editing**. Activate it by pressing `O` or clicking the icon that looks like a target with a circle around it in the 3D Viewport header. When active, transforming a selected component will also affect nearby unselected components, with the influence gradually falling off based on a defined radius. You can adjust this radius with the scroll wheel of your mouse after initiating a transform (e.g., `G` then scroll). Blender offers different **falloff types** (e.g., Smooth, Sphere, Root, Sharp, Linear, Constant, Random) which dictate how the influence diminishes. "Smooth" is excellent for natural, organic shapes like terrain or character muscles, while "Sharp" or "Linear" might be used for more controlled, angular deformations.

Common mistakes often involve forgetting to turn off Proportional Editing, leading to unintended widespread deformations. Always check the Proportional Editing icon or press `O` to toggle it. Another frequent issue is having the wrong pivot point selected; if your rotation or scale isn't behaving as expected, check your pivot point setting. In game development, clean, smooth deformations are vital for animated characters and realistic environments, making Proportional Editing an indispensable tool for achieving natural forms. For example, shaping a mountain range or a character's bicep would heavily rely on proportional editing to ensure smooth transitions.

screens.title: Basic Transformation & Manipulation in Edit Mode
screens.subtitle: Move, rotate, scale selected vertices, edges, and faces with precision and organic control.

narration.text: In this chapter we focus on transforming parts of a mesh while in Edit Mode. You will learn to move, rotate, and scale selected vertices, edges, and faces with the same tools used in Object Mode, but with much finer control because the operations apply only to your selection. We will cover axis constraints, how the transformation orientation affects the result, and the practical role of pivot points such as the Median Point, Active Element, Individual Origins, the 3D Cursor, and the Bounding Box Center. Finally, we'll introduce Proportional Editing, which lets a transform gracefully influence nearby geometry to create organic shapes. Together these skills let you tweak a character's brow, shape a barrel stave, or sculpt a terrain hill with predictable results. As you work, watch out for common mistakes like leaving Proportional Editing on or using the wrong pivot point. By the end of this chapter you will be able to pick the right pivot, orientation, and falloff to get the deformation you intend. Ready to practice precise, intentional edits on a subdivided plane and real meshes? Let’s begin by setting expectations and then dive step by step into each tool and setting.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Edit Mode transforms affect only selected mesh components — choose orientation, pivot, and falloff to control how those edits behave.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll build and why they matter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to apply foundational Edit Mode transformations to selected mesh components and make intentional modeling choices. First, you will use Move, Rotate, and Scale on vertices, edges, and faces to adjust form at a detailed level — an essential skill for cleaning topology or shaping features. Second, you'll distinguish Global and Local transformation orientations. Global aligns to the world axes, which is predictable for broad adjustments, while Local aligns to a component's own axes and is critical for moving an angled face outward from its surface. Third, you'll learn to pick the right pivot point for a task, such as using Individual Origins to scale many staves independently or the 3D Cursor to rotate around a custom center. Finally, you'll begin using Proportional Editing to create organic changes; you will learn to adjust its radius and experiment with falloff types to achieve smooth hills or sharp creases. These four capabilities together let you shape game assets and characters reliably. We'll also show simple checks to avoid common mistakes like leaving proportional editing enabled or using an unexpected pivot. Practice will focus on a subdivided plane and small object groups to make these skills repeatable.

keyIdea.text: Master basic transforms, orientation choices, pivot selection, and proportional editing to model both precise details and organic shapes.

You will learn to recognize when Proportional Editing is still active and how leaving it enabled can cause unintended, broad deformations. You will pick the proper pivot point when the transform seems to behave oddly; for example, understanding why a rotation uses the Median Point or an Active Element can explain surprising motion. Building these low-friction checks into your workflow reduces mistakes and speeds modeling, especially in game art where predictable deformation is essential.

screens.title: Move, Rotate, Scale in Edit Mode
screens.subtitle: How the same tools behave on selected vertices, edges, and faces

narration.text: The basic transform trio — Move, Rotate, Scale — works in Edit Mode just like in Object Mode, but the effect is applied only to what you have selected: vertices, edges, or faces. Move is invoked with the G key. When you press it, you grab the selected elements and can drag them freely, or constrain the move by pressing a single axis key, such as the X, Y, or Z key, to restrict motion. Rotate is R and rotates around the current pivot, which we will examine in later lessons. Scale is S and scales relative to the pivot as well. A concrete example: to deepen an eye socket, select the ring of vertices around the eye and press S to scale inward, or G then Z to move them along the Z-axis. Notice that the selection’s topology and adjacency matter; moving a vertex can stretch connected faces and alter surface normals. A common misconception is that transforming components in Edit Mode preserves the object's origin. It does — only the selected geometry moves; the object origin and other unselected vertices remain unchanged. Practice this on a small cube or a subdivided plane until you reliably constrain transforms and see how connected geometry reacts. After that, we'll layer orientation and pivot choices on top so your edits behave exactly as you intend.

keyIdea.title: Essential claim
keyIdea.text: Edit Mode transforms affect only selected components; axis constraints refine movement and the pivot determines rotation and scaling center.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Move / Rotate / Scale
Definition
Transform tools in Edit Mode

Move (G): grab and translate selected components. Constrain with axis keys.

Rotate (R): rotate selection around the current pivot.

Scale (S): scale selection relative to pivot; axis constraints apply.

Example
Select vertices around an eye and use S to scale them inward to deepen the socket; use G then Z to move inward on the Z-axis for finer control.
Key Takeaway

Transformations apply only to selected components, so plan selections to prevent unwanted distortion.

Large visual: Transform examples
Annotated steps
Move (Translate)
  • Press the G key to grab selection.
  • Press X / Y / Z to constrain to an axis.
  • Confirm or press Esc to cancel.
Scale & Rotate
  • S scales relative to pivot; use axis keys to scale on one axis.
  • R rotates around pivot; use an axis key to lock rotation axis.
Practical tip
When moving connected vertices expect adjacent faces to stretch; undo and adjust selection if topology looks wrong.

screens.title: Axis Constraints and Precise Control
screens.subtitle: Lock transforms to X, Y, Z or use two-axis constraints for finer edits

narration.text: Axis constraints let you control exactly which direction a transform moves or scales. When you start a transform, press one of the axis keys — X, Y, or Z — to lock the action to that axis. This reduces the chance of slipping along an unintended direction, which is especially useful for maintaining symmetry or keeping vertices aligned to a grid. You can also combine axis choices in many workflows: after pressing S to scale, pressing Shift plus an axis key will exclude that axis, allowing a scale on the two remaining axes. For example, press S then Shift Z to scale on X and Y only, preserving height. A concrete scenario: if you're widening a belt on a character but must keep its thickness, use S then Shift Z to scale only horizontally and longitudinally. A frequent misconception is that axis constraints always snap to a world axis. Remember that axis behavior depends on the current transformation orientation; Global locks to the world axes, while Local follows a component or object's axes. Practicing these constraints makes iterative edits quick and precise, especially when combined with careful selection and the correct pivot point. Try constraining and then using the 3D Cursor pivot for special rotation centers in later steps.

keyIdea.title: Actionable tip
keyIdea.text: Use axis constraints to limit transforms and combine them with Shift to exclude an axis for two-axis transforms.

content.html:

  2. Press X, Y, or Z to lock to that axis.
  3. Use Shift + axis to exclude an axis when scaling.
  4. Combine with orientation choices for local alignment.

screens.title: Transformation Orientation: Global vs Local
screens.subtitle: When to use world axes and when to align to component normals

narration.text: Transformation orientation determines how axis constraints behave and how transforms rotate or scale relative to geometry. Global orientation aligns to the scene's fixed X, Y, and Z axes. This is useful when you want absolute, predictable motion across your scene — for example, sliding a rooftop piece along the world X axis so it matches other buildings. Local orientation, by contrast, aligns the transform axes with the selected component's or object's own axes. Practically, Local is essential when working on angled faces: if you want to push a face directly outward along its normal, Local will align the Z axis to that face, letting you move or scale outward cleanly. A common misconception is that Local always matches the object's rotation; in Edit Mode, Local can align to the active element or selection orientation depending on context. Try this: select an angled face and use Global to move along world Z, then switch to Local to move along the face's normal. The difference is immediate — one moves straight up in world space, the other moves directly out from the surface. Understanding orientation prevents subtle errors when aligning elements on curved or angled geometry.

keyIdea.title: Why orientation matters
keyIdea.text: Choose Global for scene-aligned edits and Local for surface-aligned edits; mismatched orientation is a frequent source of confusion.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Transformation Orientation
Global
World-aligned axes
Use Global when you need transformations that align to the scene coordinate system. It is predictable and consistent across objects.
Example
Move a roof section along the scene X axis to align with neighboring buildings.
Local
Component or object-aligned axes
Use Local to move a face along its normal or rotate an element according to its own orientation. This is invaluable on angled surfaces.
Quick check
If you expect motion along a face's outward direction, switch to Local; if motion is scene-global, stay with Global.
Misconception
Local always equals object rotation — not quite. In Edit Mode Local often aligns to selection or active element orientation. Verify the selected orientation before committing a transform.

screens.title: Pivot Points: What they do
screens.subtitle: Choose the center for rotations and scales to control transform behavior

narration.text: A pivot point determines the center about which rotations and scales occur. Choosing the correct pivot is often the difference between an edit that preserves a design and one that breaks alignment. The common pivot choices are Median Point, Active Element, Individual Origins, 3D Cursor, and Bounding Box Center. Median Point calculates the average center of all selected components and is often the default because it yields an intuitive center for grouped selections. Active Element uses the last selected component as the pivot — useful when you want the rest of a selection to rotate around a specific vertex or face. Individual Origins makes each selected component use its own center, so multiple items rotate or scale independently; this is perfect for scaling staves of a barrel outward while preserving their individual centers. The 3D Cursor acts as a user-placed pivot; move the cursor somewhere precise and transforms happen about that point. Bounding Box Center uses the center of the selection's axis-aligned bounding box, which can differ subtly from the median. A common pitfall is expecting a rotation to use the object origin — a pivot mismatch is usually the cause. Practice switching pivots while observing the outcome to internalize each option's effect.

keyIdea.title: Pivot principle
keyIdea.text: Set the pivot intentionally; it controls rotation and scale centers and therefore the overall geometry outcome.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Pivot Points
Median Point
Average center of the selection; predictable for grouped edits.
Active Element
Last selected component becomes the pivot. Great for aligning other elements to one reference.
Individual Origins
Each selection rotates or scales around its own center. Use for repeated elements or arrays.
3D Cursor
Place the 3D Cursor and use it as a custom pivot for precise control.
Bounding Box Center
Center of the smallest axis-aligned box that encloses your selection; similar to Median but computed differently.
Pro tip

If your rotation looks wrong, check the pivot. Often switching between Median and Active Element resolves unexpected motion.

screens.title: Median Point vs Active Element
screens.subtitle: How the last selected item influences transforms

narration.text: Median Point and Active Element are two pivot choices that look similar at first but serve different purposes. Median Point computes the average center of the entire selection. If you select multiple vertices, edges, or faces, the Median gives you a balanced center, which is useful for evenly distributed edits. Active Element designates the last selected component as the pivot. This matters when you want the rest of your selection to behave relative to a single reference. For example, imagine aligning spikes around a central face: select all spike bases, make the intended central face the last selection to make it active, and rotate — the spikes will pivot around that active face. A common mistake is expecting Active Element to be visually obvious; it is the last selected and typically highlighted brighter. Always confirm which is active before rotating. Practice this by selecting a row of cubes or faces, toggling between Median and Active Element, and observing how the rotation or scale changes. The difference becomes intuitive after a few tries and is a key control when aligning multiple components to a reference.

keyIdea.title: Contrast
keyIdea.text: Median averages the selection; Active uses one explicit reference as the pivot — choose based on whether you need a neutral center or a specific anchor.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Median vs Active
Median Point (Example)
Select several vertices and rotate — the group rotates around their average center.
Use case
Centering a cluster of faces or rotating a selection symmetrically.
Active Element (Example)
Make one vertex or face active last, then rotate; the whole selection uses that active as the pivot.
Use case
Aligning multiple pieces to a chosen anchor or snapping others to one element.
Check your understanding
If a selection rotates around a surprising point, was the desired anchor selected last? If not, switch to Active Element and reselect in the correct order.

narration.text: Individual Origins and Bounding Box Center offer two distinct behaviors for grouped transforms. Individual Origins treats each selected element as its own pivot; each piece rotates or scales around its own center independently. This is excellent when you have repeated elements — like barrel staves — and you want to scale each stave outward while keeping the barrel's overall silhouette. The Bounding Box Center computes the center of the axis-aligned box that encloses the selection and uses that as the pivot. It can be similar to the Median Point but differs because it is axis-aligned and influenced by outlier geometry that shifts the box. Choose Bounding Box Center when you need a consistent, axis-aligned center for a group, such as scaling an array so it grows uniformly in all directions from its bounding center. A beginner mistake is using Individual Origins when you intended a single central pivot; the result looks like each element moved on its own. Try both settings on a selection of cubes and watch how each cube scales under Individual Origins but together scale from a uniform center when Bounding Box Center is chosen.

keyIdea.title: When to use each
keyIdea.text: Use Individual Origins for independent element edits and Bounding Box Center for a uniform group center that respects axis alignment.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Individual Origins / Bounding Box
Individual Origins
Each selection rotates/scales on its own pivot.
Example
Scale many staves to bow them independently while the group remains in place.
Bounding Box Center
Use the selection's axis-aligned bounding box center as pivot.
Example
Scale an array of objects outward from the box center to grow a grid uniformly.
Common mistake
If each element moves independently when you wanted a single center, you likely have Individual Origins selected by accident.

screens.title: Using the 3D Cursor as a Pivot
screens.subtitle: Place the cursor precisely and transform around that point

narration.text: The 3D Cursor is a flexible, user-placed pivot point. You place it where you want and then choose the 3D Cursor pivot to perform rotations or scales around that exact location. To set the cursor quickly, use Shift plus a right-click in Blender's default interaction scheme. Once positioned, choose the 3D Cursor pivot mode and start your transform. This is useful when you need a pivot outside the selection or at a specific offset — for instance, rotating a door around its hinge point that lies outside the currently selected vertices. A practical example: select the edge of a panel, place the 3D Cursor at the hinge location, and rotate the panel around that cursor to simulate opening. Be mindful that the cursor persists until moved, so unintended pivots can occur if you forget to reset it. A common pitfall is assuming the 3D Cursor snaps to geometry by default; you must place it explicitly. Use the 3D Cursor when other pivots don't offer the specific center you need, and remember to move it back or switch pivot mode after finishing the specialized edit.

keyIdea.title: 3D Cursor use
keyIdea.text: Place the 3D Cursor for precise, custom pivots when standard pivot points don't match your required center.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › 3D Cursor Pivot
How to use
  1. Place the 3D Cursor at the intended pivot location (Shift + Right-Click by default).
  2. Select the 3D Cursor pivot mode from the viewport header.
  3. Start the transform and the action will use the cursor as center.
Example
Rotate a panel around an external hinge by placing the cursor at the hinge, then rotating the panel to simulate opening.
Common pitfalls
  • Forgetting to move the cursor after a specialized edit. It remains in place until changed.
  • Assuming the cursor snaps automatically to geometry; it must be placed deliberately.
Key Takeaway

Use the 3D Cursor for custom pivots that other built-in pivots cannot provide.

screens.title: Proportional Editing Basics
screens.subtitle: A radius-based influence to create smooth, organic deformations

narration.text: Proportional Editing lets a transformation applied to selected components also influence nearby unselected geometry. Toggle it on and off with the O key or the viewport icon. When active, a transform will pull or push neighboring vertices with a falling influence determined by a radius. You can change the radius during a transform using the scroll wheel, expanding or contracting the area of effect. This is invaluable for creating gentle hills, muscle bulges, or terrain features — anything that benefits from a smooth gradient of movement rather than sharp, isolated edits. Blender provides several falloff types such as Smooth, Sphere, Root, Sharp, Linear, Constant, and Random. Smooth generally gives the most natural organic result; Sharp tightens the influence near the selection for more pronounced edits. A common error is forgetting proportional editing is still active and making unintended broad changes later. Always glance at the Proportional Editing icon. To practice, select a single vertex on a subdivided plane, enable proportional editing, and use the scroll wheel during a move to feel how the radius changes the surrounding geometry. Observing how connected topology reacts will help you pick the right falloff for your artistic goal.

keyIdea.title: Proportional Editing
keyIdea.text: Use proportional editing with an appropriate falloff and radius to create natural, gradual deformations across a mesh.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Proportional Editing
Toggle and control
Toggle with the O key. Start a transform, then use the mouse wheel to adjust the radius interactively.
Falloff types
  • Smooth — natural curves for organic shapes.
  • Sphere — rounded influence similar to Smooth.
  • Sharp / Linear — for tighter, more defined influence.
Practical example
On a subdivided plane, select one vertex, enable proportional editing, and lift it up while scrolling to expand the radius. Observe how the surrounding vertices rise with a soft falloff to form a hill.
Common mistake
Leaving proportional editing enabled will change unrelated parts of the mesh. Confirm the icon state before performing precise edits.
Key Takeaway

Proportional editing lets one edit affect many vertices smoothly; pick falloff and radius to match the desired organic effect.

screens.title: Falloff Types and Radius Control
screens.subtitle: How different falloffs change the influence curve

narration.text: Falloff type defines the mathematical curve that determines how influence decreases with distance from the selection. Smooth produces a gradual bell-like curve, which is great for natural terrain and soft body forms. Sphere gives a rounded influence similar to Smooth but often with a slightly different spatial distribution. Root can give a stronger center and gentler outer influence, while Sharp or Linear makes the influence drop off more abruptly, useful when you want a pronounced ridge or crease. Constant applies equal influence inside the radius, producing a flat-topped effect, and Random adds jitter for noisy surfaces. The radius controls how far this influence reaches; increasing it affects more vertices, creating broader, softer changes. During a transform, use the mouse wheel to change the radius interactively and watch how the affected ring grows and fades. A practical exercise is to create one hill with Smooth falloff for a rolling terrain and then switch to Sharp to make a sharper ridge on the same mesh. This direct comparison clarifies when each falloff best supports your artistic intent and helps avoid selecting the wrong falloff for the desired shape.

keyIdea.title: Falloff insight
keyIdea.text: Match falloff to intent: Smooth for natural transitions, Sharp for defined creases, Constant for flat influence, and Random for noise.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Falloff & Radius
Smooth
Gentle, natural curves for organic shapes.
Sharp / Linear
Tighter, more defined influence for ridges and creases.
Constant / Random
Flat or noisy influence for stylized or rough surfaces.
Try this
Create one feature using Smooth, then reapply with Sharp to compare results. Use the scroll wheel during each transform to preview radius changes and choose the smallest radius that achieves a natural transition.

screens.title: Activity: Sculpt a Simple Terrain Hill
screens.subtitle: Subdivide a plane, enable Proportional Editing, and shape a hill and crater

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks through creating a terrain hill using the exact steps from the chapter. Start a new file, delete the default cube, and add a plane. Subdivide the plane heavily — increase the number of cuts to twenty or thirty — to give enough geometry for smooth deformation. Enter Edit Mode, make sure you are in Vertex Select mode, and select a central vertex where you want the hill to rise. Press the O key to enable Proportional Editing and choose Smooth falloff. Press the G key to grab the vertex and then press Z to constrain movement to the vertical axis. Use your mouse wheel while moving the vertex to increase the proportional radius until surrounding vertices lift gradually into a hill. To make a crater, select another vertex and move it downwards with proportional editing still active. Experiment with different falloff types like Sphere or Sharp to see how the shape changes. Finally, try selecting a row of vertices, change the pivot to Individual Origins, and scale along Z to produce repeated, independent adjustments. This activity gives you immediate, visible feedback on how radius and falloff shape the mesh and trains you to check pivot and proportional state before each transform.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Practice proportional editing and pivot choices on a subdivided plane to learn falloff behavior and radius control.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Terrain Hill Activity
Step-by-step checklist
  1. Add a Plane and Subdivide with 20–30 cuts.
  2. Enter Edit Mode and select a central vertex.
  3. Press O to enable Proportional Editing and pick Smooth falloff.
  4. Press G then Z and use the mouse wheel to set the radius and lift the hill.
  5. Create a crater by moving another vertex downwards with proportional editing.
Try variations
Switch falloff types to see differences and experiment with Individual Origins on a row of vertices for independent scaling.
Example operator panel notes
Subdivide → Number of Cuts: 20
Enable Proportional Editing → Falloff: Smooth
Select vertex → G then Z → Mouse wheel to change radius
Use these operator settings as a quick reference while you practice the activity in Blender.

screens.title: Avoiding Mistakes & Practical Checks
screens.subtitle: Quick checks to keep transforms predictable

narration.text: Transform-related mistakes are usually small, but they can cost time. Build three quick checks into your workflow. First, confirm which pivot is selected: Median, Active, Individual Origins, 3D Cursor, or Bounding Box Center. If rotation or scale looks wrong, switching the pivot often fixes it immediately. Second, check the transformation orientation — Global versus Local. If an axis constraint moves your selection in an unexpected direction, verify orientation before undoing the operation. Third, look at the Proportional Editing icon; leaving it on can spread edits widely and silently. A common bad habit is making several edits without noticing a stray proportional radius or an accidental active element. When things go wrong, use undo to step back, inspect the pivot/orientation/proportional state, and replay the transform deliberately. Another practical tip: practice on a subdivided plane or a duplicate object when experimenting with falloff and pivot combinations. This reduces risk to your primary asset and speeds learning. These checks will reduce surprises and help you produce clean, deformation-ready geometry for animation or game use. narration.text: Keep three concise ideas in mind as you practice transformations. First, transformations in Edit Mode apply only to the selected vertices, edges, or faces, so selection strategy determines the result. Second, choose orientation and pivot intentionally: Global vs Local controls the axes you lock to, and the pivot point determines the center for rotation and scale. Third, proportional editing is a radius-driven influence tool that, when used with an appropriate falloff type, produces organic, smooth deformations. These ideas interact: an axis-constrained move with the wrong pivot or an unexpected proportional radius will produce surprising outcomes. Use the quick checklist — pivot, orientation, proportional — before every important transform. When you master these three, you will make more predictable, intentional edits and avoid common modeling errors in animation and game asset production.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three actionable reminders before you edit

narration.text: Keep this short checklist in mind before every transform. First, confirm your selection: only selected vertices, edges, or faces will move. Second, decide which pivot you need: Median for balanced centers, Active for anchoring to one element, Individual Origins for independent edits, the 3D Cursor for custom pivots, or Bounding Box Center for axis-aligned group centers. Third, toggle Proportional Editing deliberately and choose the falloff and radius that match your intent. These three reminders — selection, pivot, proportional — form a reliable pre-transform routine that prevents accidental deformations and speeds your modeling workflow. Before you finish, reflect on when you would prefer Individual Origins over the Median Point and try both on a simple grid to see the difference. This short mental checklist will make your edits intentional and reproducible across projects.
